content: Pluralistic ignorance, privately doubting a norm that everyone publicly upholds, is a genuine and reasonably well-supported phenomenon; the classic demonstration is Prentice & Miller (1993), who found college students systematically overestimated their peers' comfort with heavy drinking. So this part stands on firmer ground than the line-judging studies it is bolted onto. Worth noting the two are distinct mechanisms: Asch conformity is about yielding to a visible majority in the moment, while pluralistic ignorance is a shared misperception of others' private attitudes. They can co-occur but neither requires the other, and the essay's seamless merge slightly overstates how much Asch's task tells us about real-world norm suppression.
